A.explanation: Too small by a factor of about 100, consistent with a mistake in converting $14 \text{ MW}$ or in using $\sin 0.64^\circ$.

B.explanation: Too small by a factor of about 10, consistent with using $0.64$ radians instead of $0.64^\circ$ or a power-of-ten error.

C.explanation: Driving force $F = mg\sin 0.64^\circ$ divided into $P = 14 \times 10^6 \text{ W}$ gives $v \approx 39 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

D.explanation: Too large by a factor of about 10, consistent with omitting $\sin 0.64^\circ$ correctly or confusing mass with weight.

hints: Notice the train moves at constant speed up the $0.64^\circ$ slope with no friction, so the forward driving force must exactly balance the component of weight down the slope.
Recall the two linked relations: component of weight along the slope is $mg\sin\theta$ and useful mechanical power is $P = Fv$.
Calculate $F = (3.3 \times 10^6) \times 9.81 \times \sin 0.64^\circ$ in newtons, then rearrange to $v = P/F$ with $P = 14 \times 10^6 \text{ W}$.
walkthrough: List the useful data: $m = 3.3 \times 10^6 \text{ kg}$, $\theta = 0.64^\circ$, $P = 14 \text{ MW} = 14 \times 10^6 \text{ W}$, and $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Use constant velocity to find the required force. Resultant force is zero, so driving force $F$ equals the weight component down the slope: $F = mg\sin\theta$.
Use the power relation for motion with force parallel to velocity: $P = Fv$, so $v = P/F = P/(mg\sin\theta)$.
Substitute values with units: $F = (3.3 \times 10^6 \text{ kg})(9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2})\sin 0.64^\circ \approx 3.6 \times 10^5 \text{ N}$.
Then $v = (14 \times 10^6 \text{ W})/(3.6 \times 10^5 \text{ N}) \approx 39 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ with unit $\text{W N}^{-1} = \text{m s}^{-1}$. This is option C.
